ちょっと トイレを 借[か]りたいんですが？
May I use your restroom?/May I borrow the restroom?
Travel
ちょっと (chotto) means "a little" or "a moment," トイレ (toire) means "restroom," 借りたい (karitai) means "want to borrow," and んですが (n desu ga) is a polite way to soften the request.
どんな 本[ほん]が 好[す]き？
What kind of books do you like?
Emotion
料金[りょうきん]は いくらですか?
How much is the fare?
Travel
料金 (りょうきん, ryōkin) means "fare," and いくらですか (ikura desu ka) means "how much?"
以上[いじょう]で よろしいですか？
Is this all right?
Travel
以上 (ijou) means "above" or "this is all." よろしい (yoroshii) is a polite form of よい (yoi), meaning "good" or "acceptable." ですか (desu ka) turns the sentence into a polite question.
料金[りょうきん]は おいくらですか？
How much is the fare?
Travel
料金 (りょうきん, ryōkin) means "fare" or "charge." おいくら (oikura) means "how much" in a polite form. です (desu) is the copula, and か (ka) turns it into a question.

この 建物[たてもの]は いつから ありますか？
How long has this building been there?
鼠,Travel
英語[えいご]が 話[はな]せます
I can speak English
Travel

The verb 話せます (hanasemasu) is the polite form of the potential verb, meaning "can speak." All verbs when conjuated into the potential "can" form use the が particle even if they would usually use the を particle.
英語[えいご]が 話[はな]せますか
Can you speak English?
Travel
The question form of the sentence, asking if someone can speak English. The か (ka) particle turns the statement into a question.
あなたは 特別[とくべつ]な 人[ひと]。
You're a special person.
Emotion
どんな 音楽[おんがく]が 好[す]き？
What kind of music do you like?
Emotion
入場[にゅうじょう]料[りょう] はいりますか？
Is there an entrance fee?
Travel
入場料 (にゅうじょうりょう, nyūjōryō) means "entrance fee," and いりますか (irimasu ka) asks if something is required.
この 料理[りょうり]は 何[なん]ですか？
What is this dish?
鼠,Travel
この 建物[たてもの]は 何[なん]ですか？
What is this building?
Travel
この (kono) means "this," 建物 (たてもん, tatemono) means "building," and 何 (なん, nan) means "what," with ですか (desu ka) making the question.
料理[りょうり]が まだ 来[き]ていません
The food hasn't come yet.
Travel

料理 (ryōri) means "food" or "dish." が (ga) is the subject marker, indicating that "food" is the subject of the sentence. まだ (mada) means "yet" or "still," implying that something has not happened up to that point. 来ていません (kite imasen) is the negative form of 来る (kuru), meaning "to come," with いません (imasen) being the polite negative ending. This phrase politely informs that the food has not arrived yet.
ここに 入[はい]るのは 有料[ゆうりょう]ですか？
Do I have to pay to enter here?
鼠,Travel
お土産[みやげ]は どこで 売[う]ってますか？
Where are souvenirs sold?
鼠,Travel
お土産[みやげ]は どこで 売[う]っていますか？
Where are souvenirs sold?
Travel
お土産 (おみやげ, omiyage) means "souvenir," and this question asks where souvenirs can be purchased.
自分[じぶん]で 自分[じぶん]の どんな ところが 好[す]き？
What do you like about yourself?
Emotion
ベジタリアン用[よう]の 料理[りょうり]が ありますか？
Do you have vegetarian dishes?
Travel
ベジタリアン用 (bejitarian-yō) means "for vegetarians," 料理 (ryōri) means "dishes," and ありますか (arimasu ka) is a polite way of asking "Is there?"
もちろんです。 試着[しちゃく]室[しつ]は こちらです。
Of course. The fitting room is over here.
鼠,Travel
この あたりの ご飯[はん]屋[や]を 教[おし]えてください。
Please let me know about the restaurants in this area.
鼠,Travel
ここから 日本[にほん]への フライトは １[いち]日[にち] １[いち] 便[びん]しか ない。
There is only one flight per day from here to Japan.
Counter,Common

便 · びん · 便 is used to count the number of flights, boats shipping out, long-distance buses, etc. over a period of time. It can also be used as an ordinal number suffix for delivery or transportation. If you're referring to a flight number, for example, you could use this ordinal number suffix.

Is there anyone who can speak English?
Travel

英語 (えいご, eigo) means "English" (the language), 話せる (はなせる, hanaseru) is the potential form of the verb "to speak" (話す, はなす, hanasu), meaning "can speak." 人 (ひと, hito) means "person," and いますか (いますか, imasu ka) is a polite question form asking if someone is present.

前菜[ぜんさい]は ３[さん]品[ぴん] ご用意[ようい] しております。
We prepared three dishes for the appetizer.
Counter,Common

品 · しな/ひん · 品 is used to count items, products, or dishes of food. In situations where it's pronounced しな, you'll want to use the wago counting method for one (一品/ひとしな) and two (二品/ふたしな). After that it's all kango. When pronounced as ひん, this counter just uses the kango counting method right from the start.
すみませんが 質問[しつもん]が あるんですが
Excuse me, but I have a question.
Travel
すみませんが (sumimasen ga) means "excuse me," 質問 (shitsumon) means "question," and ある (aru) means "to have" or "to exist", and んですか (desu ka) makes it polite.
ペンを １[いっ]本[ぽん] 貸[か]してくれませんか？

Counter,Must Know
本 · ほん · Stick-shaped or long things.

Where is the nearest ATM?

一番 (ichiban) means "number one" and 近い (chikai) means "close," so 一番 近い (ichiban chikai) means "nearest" or "closest," and どこですか (doko desu ka) asks "where is it?"

今日[きょう]は トマト １[いち]玉[たま] ２１[にじゅういち]円[えん]ですって。

Counter,Common

玉 · たま · Round things, such as tomatoes, peaches, heads of lettuce, cabbage, and of course, testicles. It can also be used to count tangled balls of string, and other "ball-shaped" things, even if they're not ball-shaped when taken apart. For example, a ball of yarn could be counted with 玉. Or even a portion of noodles. Instead of 玉, though, it's probably more common to use the general counter 個. One exception to this is pachinko balls, which are pretty much always counted with 玉, no matter what. For one or two balls, use the wago counting method (ひとたま, ふたたま). After that, it's all kango all the way.

これを 温[あたた]めてください
Please warm this up
Travel
A polite request to heat something. これ (kore) means "this," 温めて (atatamete) is the te-form of the verb "to warm," and ください (kudasai) means "please."
助[たす]けてもらえますか？
Can you help me?
Travel

"助けて" is the te-form of the verb "助ける" (to help), "もらえますか" is a polite way of asking if someone is able to do something for you. The phrase uses the potential form "もらえます" to ask if it's possible for someone to help. The sentence is a polite request for assistance.
もちろん、 助[たす]けます。
Of course, I will help.
Travel
もちろん (mochiron) means "of course" or "certainly." 助けます (tasukemasu) is the polite form of "to help."

コストコで オムツを ３[さん] 箱[ばこ] 買[か]った。

Counter,Common

箱 · はこ · Boxes. Pretty much any kind is fine. Boxes of diapers, sponge cake, snacks, tea leaves, etc. The only exception to this is small disposable wooden/cardboard boxes filled with sweets, a meal, or bento. These are counted with 折 (おり). When counting with 箱, use wago or kango for one and two. Sometimes use wago for three boxes, but mostly stick with kango. From four and above, use the kango counting method.

Counter,Common

皿 · さら · 皿 means "dish" or "plate," referring to dishes or plates of food. For empty plates, you can still use 皿, but the counter 枚 will be more common for this. If you want to count individual pieces of food on the plate, you'll want to use 品 (しな). You can use 皿 to count laboratory dishes as well (like the ones that grow bacteria). For one and two plates, use the wago reading (ひとさら、ふたさら). Three can be either (みさら or さんさら). From four on up, just use kango.

名 · めい · 名 is a counter for counting people that's more polite than the other person counter, 人. Another difference is that 名 can't be used as an ordinal number suffix like 人 can, so don't try to count the first, second, third (etc.) person. With this one, all you can do is count the number of people.
